title: BSKDL Basisschrift Computerbraille Insert and Six-Dot Transport Contract

commonMappingTable.description: Expanded representation of the section 2.11 list of frequently used Computerbraille signs.

rules.summary: E-mail addresses, URLs and text containing computer character-set words or strings are normally represented in Computerbraille for unambiguous transcription.
Computerbraille is primarily an eight-dot Braille system in which one character is represented by one Braille cell.
When eight-dot Computerbraille inserts are not possible, Computerbraille characters are serialized through the section 2.11 six-dot transport technique.
A Computerbraille cell containing neither dot 7 nor dot 8 normally retains its dots 1 through 6 unchanged.
Dot 7 is replaced by a preceding dot-4 cell while dots 1 through 6 remain in the following six-dot cell.
Dot 8 is replaced by a preceding dot-6 cell while dots 1 through 6 remain in the following six-dot cell.
Dots 7 and 8 together are replaced by a preceding dots-4-6 cell.
Computerbraille characters consisting only of dot 4, dot 6, or dots 4-6 are doubled to prevent confusion with transport prefixes.
A Computerbraille insert whose serialized form contains no Braille blank uses the no-blank announcement marker.
A Computerbraille insert whose serialized form contains at least one Braille blank uses the blank-containing announcement marker.
A blank created while serializing a source cell consisting only of dot 7, dot 8, or dots 7-8 counts when selecting the insert announcement marker.
The Computerbraille announcement marker is placed immediately before the first encoded Computerbraille sign.
The Computerbraille terminator is placed immediately after the final encoded sign, including after an encoding blank that forms part of a two-cell representation.
When a Computerbraille passage does not fit on a line, breaking at a real content blank is preferred where possible.
When a suitable real blank is unavailable, a line may end with dot 4 as the Computerbraille continuation separator.
Two-cell Computerbraille transport forms must not be split across lines.
Section 2.11 provides a list of frequently used Computerbraille signs in six-dot form; the list must not be interpreted as a complete Computerbraille character-set specification.
